SCHOOLS IN JACKSON COUNTY

The first organized school in Kansas was organized in Wyandotte by J.M. Armstrong in 1844. It lasted until his death in 1852. The school had the distinction of being the first established for white children in what is now the state of Kansas. A school for whites was established in Council Grove in 1851 by Mr. T.S. Huffaker. The State of Kansas is challenged to find another county surpassing Jackson in its zealous devotion to educational matters.
Shortly after the county was organized in 1857, the people began to think about schools for their children.

The first school was taught in this county by Miss Hariet Warfield of Clay County Missouri in 1857. It was gotten up on the subscription plan, and held in a little log cabin, 10 feet square, located on the SW 1/4 section 23, township 9, range 16. This would put about 5 miles east of Hoyt. (1)
School was started in Jefferson township the same year. Mrs. H.S. Hart held school in her log cabin.
Hard times, drought, the coming of the Civil War and the internal strife in Kansas kept the people of Jackson County from doing much about schools until after 1861. (1)

The first real school was built in the county in 1858. It was built out of logs and was also used as a church. Information from the Kansas State Historical Society, says that the lighting came from leaving out one log in the wall on one side. It was heated by a fireplace. It was taught by Miss Anna Parrot. The name of it was called Brick, and was also the first organized district in county. Permission for this was granted on June 20, 1859. It was located on land which was part of the Pottawatomie Reserve. The school term was six months, three months in spring and three in the fall.

In 1868, George and Mary Hafer donated one acre of land to the school. It was about 1/2 mile west of the log cabin. In the same Brick school was built. In one porch was W.H. Webster. He taught for seven terms. At one time there were 58 students. The building was also used as a church until a church building was completed in 1890. In 1916 the second building was torn down and a building, with a basement was erected. School was held here until it was destroyed by a tornado in 1962. The last teacher was Katherin Linehan.
(The information about Brick was Kansas Historical Society and Forest Morris family and the Everett Gibson family.)

The first school in Holton was established in 1858 with the construction of a frame building at 415 Wisconsin. Only the lower grades maintained at that time. This continued in this building until Central was completed in 1875 at the corner of 5th and New Jersey. Prof.. C.Y. Roop organized the first high school in 1880 and the first graduation was in 1881. After the establishment of high school classes, Central School was used as as as both grade and high school. The lower grades were conducted on the lower floor and high school on the upper floor. Prof. Roop served as both superintendent and only teacher for the 3 students in first high school. Colorado school was built in 1885 at the corner of 5th & Colorado Ave. Although this school has no direct relation to the hich school, it was an internal part of the Holton school system which eventually produced high school students.
The first high school in Ho1ton was built in 1906 and continued there until 1916 when Campbell College at the north edge of Holton was acquired for use as a larger high school.

At first the county was called Calhoun. On September 24,1855 Jackson County was organized. This area went to the Kansas River. In 1868 the county was divided into two counties we do not find any mention of a superintendent until 1859. He was Ira Taber. His name is signed to the first 14 districts.

In 1860 Jackson County had population of 2,297 of which 396 were of school age, 5 to 20 years old. in 1872 this had increased to 2,587, and by 1880 to 3,855. In 1872 there were 51 districts and 6 joint districts, and by 1882, this had increased to 70 with 6 joint districts. The population was greatest around Holton. POTTAWATOMIE INDIAN MISSION AND SCHOOL
JACKSON CO., KAN.

The Pottawatomie Indian School and Mission, located on the NE 1/4 S 16, T. 9, R. 14 in Jackson County started in 1872, when a two and one half story building was completed for that purpose early in the year. The site of the school was on the summit of a high grassy hill, the building facing the north and east. This location is just a short distance east of the townsite of Nadeau which is also on the same quarter section. The town consisted of a general store and trading post run by Eli Nadeau, who was also postmaster.

The school having been built a considerable distance from a natural water supply, was supplied with that requisite by means of a pumping plant installed in the valley of Big Soldier creek on the west, which pumped water into one or more large size cisterns on the school grounds located at advantageous points.

The first building used for mission and school purposes, was 30x40 feet in size, the main school roam being 22 x 40 feet in size, thoroughly seated with desks and otherwise suitably furnished. This building was two and one-half stories high. Other buildings were added from time to time as Government funds were available and necessity demanded. After being used for a number of years the school was abandoned in l9–, the only remaining structure on the school site being a thick-walled, stone guard house which as erected to care for any recalcitrant "bucks" who paid the school visit end became obnoxious. Foundations of the rest of the

(buildings?) can still he plainly traced - having been left even with the ground. A cistern or two, covered over with old lumber are yet apparently serviceable. A few scraggly trees are lonely survivors of this once busy locality. The chapel, built for the mission, stands on the slope a short distance to the west, and faces north. It has not been used for years. In 1933, when visited by the author, was being used as a sort of granary, tool house, etc, while several swarms of bees hon also preempted quarters beneath the roof also. Beside the chapel on the west, at this time, we’re several troughs, each about 10 or 12 feet long, which had been made for the use of the Indians. These troughs were fashioned from the trunk of a large hollowed out tree. The ends were boarded up so they would hold water. One authority. commenting on these receptacles, assured the party that the squaws used them for mixing their bread dough; they were also used for watering their horses and cattle, for doing the family washings and for taking baths. A few feet away, in a chicken pen, were several wooden troughs, much smaller in size, looking as old as the troughs before mentioned. These had  served as feeding receptacles and watering troughs for small pigs and poultry. While showing signs of disintegration, they looked good for a number of years service still.

Eli Nadeau had conducted a large and well stocked trading post or the Pottawatomie on be reservation for many years, on the prairie slope just to the southwest of the mission, facing upon a trail running to the south.
Nadeau was a tall, dark, squarely-built business man, the summer of 1897,

and at that time was probably between 65 and 70 years of age. Under the treaties of 1866 and 1867, between the Government and the Prairie Band or the Pottawatomie Nation, he became one of the "Business Committee" of the tribe, for the purpose of listing the members and fixing their family relations by family units, ages and names of members.

The other two members of this committee were George Young and William W. Ross. Young was a white man, formerly a citizen of Kentucky, who had become the husband of a French and Pottawatomie woman, and thus a member of the tribe. He was the father of Mrs. Frank Bourbonais, now residing upon her allotment west of the old mission, on the NW 1/4, S. 17, T. 9, R. 14 and grandfather of Mrs. OSHA Wyatt, now residing upon her allotment just across the highway west on the NW 1/4, S.18, T. 9, R. 14. William W.
Ross the other member was a white man, and reputed to be the Ross for whom the village of Roseville was named.

Under the provisions of the treaty of 1867, Nadeau went through the proceedings in the Federal court, and became a naturalized citizen, for a few months, thereafter he secured an order of that court returning him to the status of a blanket Indian. One of his sons, Joseph E. Nadeau, by his friends called "Coe" Nadeau, owns and resides upon a well improved fore facing south on the north side of Highway No.40 just in the west edge of Shawnee county, on the SE 1/4, S. 13, T. 10, R. 12, and like his father, reputed to he e vary good and conservative business man.

Too high an estimate cannot be placed on the religious, moral and practically useful influences of these schools. They not only bring the children in contact with religious and cultivated persons, but through them reach their parents and friends, who visit them. The improved health and deportment of their children and their ability to read, write, and figure for them has convinced the adults that their children are learning that which makes the white race powerful, and their affection for those placed in charge of them is a proof that they are kindly treated. Through the schools the adult Indians have learned that a regard for virtue has its reward in the respect entertained for those who practice it, and that no good thing is expected from an untruthful or immoral source. Though we do not obtain actual expressions of religious conviction, I have not a doubt but that these influences are gradually enlightening the Indians to a better conception of true religion.

Until three years ago the Prairie band had not sent their children to school or had the advantages of religious instruction, or even example, no agent or missionary having resided among them. Living within a short distance of religious white communities and almost in hearing of church-bells, they isolated themselves from the balance of their own people, and were strangers to the voices of friend-ship and advice. Hence, while within reach of inestimable knowledge, the cultivated and cherished those religious traditions and customs which deepened in their minds a dislike of revealed religion, and prejudice against those who taught it. To be learned in these traditions was a position of honor: therefore it will not seem strange that the ablest and best informed men in the tribe made these subjects

their Greatest study. These men are generally practical on other subjects, but introduce religious questions, and they become adamant. They say, "We have the Knowledge that we must hold to our belief until our Savious comes and redeems us: that any deviation or departure from it will delay his coming." This belief must be persistently attacked. To overthrow it is not the work of a month or a year. It requires incessant and prudent effort through every individual brought in contact with them in every business transaction and through every influence that can be exerted. By pursuing this course, a modification of their extreme views has already been accomplished, and when the school children, with their changed habits and different views, commence to move among them in the discharge of the duties of life, their influence, in addition to other agencies, will, I have no doubt, hasten the consummation of our hope that these Indians will accept the religion of our Saviour Jesus Christ.
M. H. NEWLIN, United States Indian Agent.
William Nicholson, Superintendent of Indian Affairs, Lawrence, Kansas.

DENISON RURAL HIGH SCHOOL
V.J. Cramer, Principal

Denison high school dates back to 1908 when an additional year of schooling was added to the school system of Denison. A part of the grade school building was used and there was only one teacher who offered four subjects: algebra, ancient history, Latin and English to the 50 pupils who were enrolled that year. At the end of the school year, these 50 pupils were wanting more knowledge and were urging that another year be added to the high school course. Thus Denison high school became a two year school and remained so until 1915 when, in accordance with advancing times and the need for still more education, another year was added.

By that time there were more classes and a greater number of students in the high school and that necessitated more room. The crowded conditions at the school was not conducive to the best work so some of the public-spirited citizens of Denison began to agitate the question of a new building. Everyone realize that a building was needed, but some felt that the community could not carry the extra burden which a new building would mean.

In 1916 the fourth year of the course was added, and now with still more subjects being offered and a still greater number of pupils coming in, something had to be done. Someone believed that the aim of a new building might be reached by means of the new rural high school system and by 1917, the New Denison Rural High School was started on the road to success. In 1918 the building was completed and school begin in it in September.
Denison Rural High School claims the honor of being the second rural high school in Jackson County.

However, though it is one of the oldest, it is still one of the best in the county., since it was well-made and has been well taken care of. Much of the credit for the latter must be given to Mr. C. E. Brown, who has kept the building in excellent condition for all about two years since its erection. In the building there are: a gymnasium, an auditorium, study hall, a good library, five recitation rooms, laboratories and each room as well equipped.

Denison High School ranks among the highest in the county and the community and students are proud of the fact that it was rated 100% in 1928. The students always make a good showing in athletic and intellectual contest and their eagerness to do so is attributed to the "old school spirit"-that fine attitude and feeling prevailing in D.R.H.S. which makes the student feel that he cannot give less than his best whatever the contest.

Dear Mr. Copeland,

/tI read any recent issue of the Holton recorder in the column by Doris Shoff, that you would like pictures or history of one room schools in Jackson County. I know that you lack either a picture or history of several schools, including Pleasant Valley, district # 8. Recently I sent a picture of that school in care of Gladys Riley so I expect you have received it by this time.

As to some history of the school, I do not know when the school located at 7 miles west of Holton was built, but I know it was previous to the year 1907 as that was the year I first attended that school, along with two of my sisters. I remember that Fisher Stauffer was a member of the school board (Mr. Stauffer was the paternal grandfather of Auswell, Thane and Lauren Stauffer) and one time after the school board had purchased and installed new desks throughout the one room, Mr. Stauffer delivered a lecture to the students about the care that should be taken of the new desks. As a parking suggestion, he said "anyone doing any carving on the new desk should be yanked out of his seat and thumped for 26 minutes." As I said, I do not know what year the school at that location was built, but I do remember my father, Ev McDonald, telling we children that previous to the building of the new school, he had attended a one room school, which was located about 1/2 mile east of the new school on the south side of the road on a part of the farm owned and occupied by the Hearn family, later the John Fisher farm, which is now owned and occupied by Fred Fischer and wife. My father told us that he remembered Elizabeth Hearn attending that school, said that she was such a tiny, dainty little girl.

There are many incidents that I remember in connection with dear Pleasant Valley school, but one I especially remember, was in connection with a custom of those days in country schools. It was such fun to go home with special friends to spend the night and one time I had gone home with a special friend and at the "supper" table that evening, the large bowl of fried potatoes was passed to me first. well, my friend had a small brother at home, not yet school age and when I was handed the dish, he said to me "don’t you take all the Brown tatie’s!". I do not remember whether or not he was reprimanded, but I think I shall never forget the incident!
Yours truly,
Evelyn (McDonald) LaMar

Here is the information I had about the early Circleville schools: The first school was held in a little log house across the road from the present site of the cemetery, and was taught by Miss Hulda Allen, who boarded with the Joseph Cook family in New Brighton. Mrs. H.S. hart taught the first school in the Township, a subscription school. It was not always easy to get money, so Mrs. Hart took her pay in any articles the people could give. Once she received a flat iron in pay, which is still in possession of her daughter Mrs. T.J. Richardson.

Later schools were held in the old Hemp house, north of the present Charles Snyder Home; Also, the old Methodist seminary, which later became the public and high school, and was torn down a few years ago.
(From Holton Recorder, March 14, 1935 written by Lillian Estee)

The seminary was built in 1865 or 1866 at a cost of $10,000. It was a beautiful limestone building and was situated at the north end of seminary Avenue, where it could be seen for miles around. It was a two-story structure, 40 x 50 and contained four large rooms. The school was divided into two departments and the first two teachers were O.C.. Allen and Miss Criselda Myers. Total enrollment was 70 peoples in the upper department and 84 in the lower. Later, it was divided into three departments. At first, the upper department provided a two-year course, but it later changed to a four-year course.

The present grade in high school building was erected in 1911, and the first junior senior banquet was held in 1915. Practically all school functions were held at either the band hall or the Methodist Church until the present auditorium and gymnasium was built in 1929. It was considered one of the most up-to-date school buildings of its time. The building was dedicated on a Friday the 13th to be used as a place of recreation, entertainment, education, etc.

THIS IS A COPY OT A LETTER WRITTEN TO ROSE WHILE SHE WAS ATTENDING CARBON GRADE SCHOOL, BY UNCLE SAM MOORE.

Dear niece: I will try and write you a few lines to help you out on your program for Valentines Day. Well, Rose, go beck with me on the stream of time to the first day in the month of October A. D. I870. In the morning along the road west from Harry Moore’s, you would have seen a tow headed boy accompanied by a young girl about three years older taking me to my first day in school.
Mr. J. Barnett was my first teacher; a man probably 65 yours old. The school hose fae called after a Mr.
Worley ,who lived where Paul Lutz resides.
The building y a non-descript affair put up out of rocks quarried close by, probably 20 ft. wide by 30 ft.

long with 3 windows and 1 door. The roof covered with home hewed shingles mostly oak. The furniture consisted of a black board, wood stove, two tables and several benches. There were no desks except a home made one for the teacher.

We had"Wilson's" reader, "Fliers" arithmetic and "Blectic"(?) speller. We used slates to write and figure on. There wore probably forty pupils enrolled the length of the winter term of school was 5 months. The summer term consisted of 3 months. Jane Richardson was the teacher--an old maid of the present day comic paper type. She punished by using a ruler on the palm of the hand of the unruly student. It usually brought tears and whimpers from him because she delighted in punishing boys.

Now back to those tables, we sat around them on benches. Each student had his place. The books and slates were piled on the table men not in use. All recitation was oral; no writing except in the penmanship class, which was of about 15 minutes duration. All spelling was done orally. All teachers of that day put a stress on the three"R's"---rending writing , spelling.
The third teacher, a Yankee, who claimed Vermont as his native state, Andy Busby was is name - about 65 years old-a failure, but Sadie Chase was extra good for two summer terms .

The next teacher was a young man named George Louis. His home was with his father (Demi Louis) who owned the farm now called, "Tudor’s Ranch". He was instrumental in securing desks and seats. The enrollment had increased up Into the 60's.

The next man teacher, Geo. Marshall, was an Ohio product. He also was first, but on account of failing health had to suspend school teaching. The summer school taught by Olie Delbert was a tame affair on account of her deciding to take steps to unite in the holy bonds of matrimony. The next one, Marian Hixon, a young man from close to Holton. Then next, Emer Rafter, a red header with a fiery temper, but with all that, a kind and generous heart. He was the idol of all the pupils. is brother Mike was the next with Jane Gileece teaching her first term of summer sohool. She stayed with us three more years.

Now you may wonder where we got so many pupils--large families--you take Ross family who lived where Mr. Iran’s lives (6 boys, 3 girls) Truman family (6 boys). The Worley family, the ones that Lived where Frank Moore Jr lives, had so many boys that he named them after the twelve apostles--used then all up then started on the twelve tribes of Israel. The Sharp family (1 girl and 5 boys). The Moore bunch, consisting of 4 boys and 2 girls of school age. Another largo family named McVey lived on Mr. Kathrens farm west of the bridge.

Now Rose, a few headlights on your school and it’s surroundings. He were visited by an army of grasshoppers in August 1875 that ate every bit of the crops that the farmer raised. The next spring they ate up the crops as fast as they came up. Finallv they left.Then we crops were replanted. It was one of the best ever raised.
The Worley schools name was changed to Carbon on account of a boom in the fancied presence of coal on the banks of Elk Creek.
"Mc Guffeys" readers, "Rays" arithmetic and "More eit" geography, "Harvey" grammar
and spelling. Also Singing and Spelling school at night and a start in Penmanship was learn.
The narrow gauge railroad was a reality. Carbon had a Post Office and for a short time a store which was moved to Holton.
Farmers started buying the upland which was owned by speculators in the east.The amount of farms was a surprise to lots of people.

Now Rose, I will go back to the teachers after Mike Rafter. John Graham, a non-descript from no where who only lasted three months. Edd Ross finished his term. After that John Preston, one of the laziest and best instructors that Carbon ever employed. With Lizzie Miller teaching the summer term Carbon was one of the leading schools of Jackson County. Preston never punished a pupil but he would talk to them which nearly always brought tears to their eyes, and they generally admitted they had done wrong and would do better in the future. Now a few side lights on his work. He was the first teacher that your grand-mother went to in Kansas......There was a young boy going to school that could not learn. He was a failure with his former teachers. He was to scape goat of all the other scholars. Preston got him started. At the and of his third term this boy was first in every book. He went to high school at Atchison, from there to Hartford. He was employed by the Santa Fe R. R. He pleased them so well that he became their best lawyer with head quarters in Chicago. His youngest brother who learned his letters under Preston is head auditor of the same railroad.

Bell Miller was a teacher in the summer term.....Now Rose, this brings us to the time when there are a few people living up there that can give you the names of other teachers that came after Preston... They can start with Ward, Bruten and your grand mother, who taught the last summer school.
Now stop and think about the past. Carbon has become grand success.
Bill Cloyse is the lawyers name.. Joseph is the auditors name.

I am a country schoolhouse. I am legion for I am found throughout this United States from East to West, and from North to South.  I stand on steep mountain sides, in canyons, in rich valleys, and on wind swept plains. I stand by the broad, paved highways that-band our land from state to state, by the seldom. traveled by-road, by the cow path that crosses the vast stretches of prairie, and by the mountain trail that wends its tortuous way up the steep slopes.
Over my threshold countless thousands of boys and girls have passed. I have been a power of force for the training of leaders in the great land of America.
In the past, my doors opened to an opportunity for educational training that was equal to the best, but not so today.
Business, Industry, commerce and transportation have marched forward in a great epoch of progress. I am a relic of the past.

Five million boys and girls cross my threshold today. They must be trained in the highest ideals of life and citizenship; they must be given the tools of the mind; they must be kept strong and stalwart in body; they must be prepared for the home-makers and the home-keepers of tomorrow; and they must be trained for leadership if America is to grow in pros-perity, in truth, and in justice. I am unequal to the task.
I need buildings that will pontect and foster the health of childbood; that w. bring children efficient tools of workmanship and will give them ideals of grace, culture, and beauty.

I need teachers of vision, teachers with a preparation for their work, teachers with a passion for children, and with a love for ine true and the beautiful, and with foresight for tomorrow's needs I need a supporting public with a social vision. with a de-sile to render service and with high ideals for themselves and their posterity.
I am the school home of five million rural boys and girls looking to the nation for equality in educational opportunity.
I AM A CHALLENGE TO THINKING AMERICA.

The Teacher "The public school teacher cannot live apart; he cannot separate his teaching from his raily walk and con-versation. He lives among his pupils during school hours, and among them and their parents all the time. He is peculiarly a public character under the most searching scrutiny of watchful and critical eyes. His life is an open book. His habits are known to all. His office, like that of a minister of religion, demands of him an exceptional standard of conduct. And how rarely does a teacher fall below that standard! How seldom does a teacher figure in a sensational headline in a newspaper! It is truly re-markable, I think, that so vast an army of people approximately eight hundred thousand — so uniformly meets its obligations, so effectively does its job, so decently behaves it-self, as to be almost utterly inconspicuous in a sensation-loving country. It implies a wealth of character, of tact, of patience, of quiet competence, to achieve such a record."-Herbert Hoover.

The Stach School was a part of the Delia community until it was moved to the grounds of the Kansas Museum of History, Topeka, in 1984. The school has been completely restored, and will be open for viewing July 4.

Delia school now historical display The Stach School, a one-room schoolhouse moved to the grounds of the Kansas Museum of History from near Delia in 1984 will open to the public- in its newly refurbished condition on July 4, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. The school, which has been restored to its 1910-1920 appearance will provide an opportunity for museum visitors to explore what education meant in rural Kansas, from about 1877, when the school was built to 1956, when it ceased to operate as a school.
A Fourth of July opening has been planned to emphasize the importance of patriotism during the decade 1910 to 1920. Lemonade and cookics, popular treats of the period, will be served to visitors.

This latest museum interpretive facility will enable visitors to experience an environment similar to that in which most Kansans, from the last half of the nineteenth century to the early decades of the twenticth century, reccived their basic education. Between 1910 and 1920, most Kansas students at-Lended onc-room schools much like the Stach School. During that pe-riod, there were over 8,700 school districts in the state; many of which consisted of one rural school. By comparison, today, as a result of the consolidation movement, there are only about 300 districts in the stale.
The school experiences of contemporary Kansas are, therefore, very different.

Initially, the Stach School will be open Sunday afternoons mid-April to mid-October from 14 p.m. with a guided tour offered free of charge at 2 p.m. The Division of Museum Education has recruited and is currently training 14 volunteer schoolhouse interpreters for this purpose.

This fall, a one-woman dramatic performance will be offcred for four consecutive weekends, Sept. 30-Oct. 21. The play, which will focus on the life of a typical rural schoolteacher of the period, will explore her relationship to students, the school board, and the commu-nity. The ticket price for each performance will include a box supper, a favorite of the period.

The Kansas Museum of History is located at 6425 SW 6th Street, Topeka, Kansas 66615, (913) 272- 8681. Major support for the Stach Schoolhouse project has been provided by Mrs. Bernice Stach Douglas and family, the Woman's Kansas Day Club, and the Institute of Museum Services.

Topeka Capital-Journal, Wednesday, October 31, 1984 Old school moves to new home By STEVE SWARTZ Capital-Journal state staff writer  -Staff/Paul Beaver STACH SCHOOL... refurbished by next summer  Bernie Douglas smiled when she thought about the 107-year-old schoolhouse that was so much a part of her childhood being preserved at the State Museum of History.

"I'm really thrilled," she said earlier this week. "I just pray that it gets down here OK." If all went according to careful planning, the old one-room school-house, built by Czechoslovakian immigrant Johr. Stach near Delia in 1877, was to arrive early today at the state museum, a department of the Kansas State Historical Society, The school was hauled to North Topeka from southwest Jackson County Tuesday and was brought pss the Kansas River and the s west side in the wee hours of today to avoid traffic. In several weeks the foundation, including some of the original rock base, will be in place at the museum and the school will be placed on it. Much of the school's roof and the belfry, which were removed for the trip to Topeka, will be put back on the old building.

Mark Hunt, museum director, said the school needs a lot of work, including painting, plaster, new roof and chimney work, and won't be open to the public until next sum-mer. The school will be placed southwest of the museum building near Urish Road.
Hunt said museum officials hope to use the buiiding to inform people how a one-room Kansas school oper-ated.

"It also was more than a school," Hunt said. "It was a community building, too." The school will be restored to represent rural education in 1915, the year the belfry, porch and cloak room were added.
"To make a proper restoration ito 1877, we'd have to eliminate those," said Hunt.

The old school was built by Stach, Douglas's grandfather, and others after a number of his fellow countrymen from the Czech provinces of Bohemia and Moravia homsteaded the area near Soldier Creek near what is now Delia. Recognizing the need for educating their children in a new land, Stach donated the land to build the school.
Between 1901 and 1907, the building was moved to a one-acre plot just north of the Shawnee Jackson county line.
In the 78 years that the school was open, 560 to 650 students attended Stach School District 59 - among them Douglas, her siblings and her parents.

Although some of her memories of attending the one-room school have faded since she graduated in 1921, she clearly recalls the Friday spelling bees and games of "Andy-over" which involved one group of children throwing a ball over the school to another mob of students.

Douglas, who at the time lived about a quarter mile from the school, also remembers the time she and the other Stach school children took the class to a "grapevine" swing in the woods during lunch time and stayed there all day.

"We decided, 'To heck with it.' We were going to stay and play," she said. "We heard that bell ringing and we thought, 'We're just not going back." When the old school closed its doors to students in April 1956, the building became a community meeting house - the Stach Community Center.

In May of 1983, when the building was to be auctioned, Douglas's cous-in, Charley Kovar, whose father purchased the land with the school site in 1922, got together with Douglas and other family members to see if the building could be preserved. An inquiry was made of the museum director, who wanted the school as an exhibit at the new museum.
With the financial aid of Douglas's son and daughter-in-law, Bob and Jan Douglas, the school was pur-chased, donated and moved to the state museum, said Hunt.
Hunt hopes eventually to make the school a living history exhibit with real people playing the roles of those who taught and were educated in the rural schools of early 20th century Kansas.

This second buildign was built by Jacob Nothacher on the same acre of land only in the north east cor-ner-where before the first building was docated in the southwest corner.

Miss Anna Pitsche opened school in September of 1907 in the new building. This building was destroyed by fire I.ring a snow storm on March 21, 1982. The remaining five weeks of school were taught in the home of Mr. and Mrs. Leonard Buehler. During the construction of the present building by. W. Vestle there was no school. A few interesting facts about Isome of the people who have lived and some who are still living in the, District are: W. A. Blossom and Walter Par-menter served on the schoolboard continuously for 25 years. Mr. S. S. Garber served for 20 years.

Mrs. Ruth Parmenter Duffy has the honor of three generations attending their entire grade school period at this school, her-self, her son Gilbert and grand. sen, Harry. Mrs. Stephen Hug sent her entire family of seven children for their complete grade school education.

Fred Blossom, who still resides in the district, has the longest residential record of any in the district, this being eighty some years. Fred received his education here as did his children, May and Orvis. Others who attended and their children were Harry Ross and his children and Leonard Buehler, his five children and three grandchildren. The Ross Tipps family have the record of the entire family, Ross, Maude, Harold and Wilma to attend Sun-rise.
